newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese yuan seen holding current level.
newsitem.headline: Chinese yuan seen holding current level.

text.p: The Chinese yuan is likely to stay at the current 8.2950-8.3000 level against the U.S. dollar for the next month on China's national foreign exchange interbank market based in Shanghai, analysts said on Monday.

There is a surplus of dollars on the market, the China Foreign Exchange Trade System, but this is likely to be offset by the central bank's determination to stabilise the local currency, the analysts said.

"The Chinese yuan will move in a narrow range around the current level of 8.2950-8.3000 in the next month," a market trader said. "Market fundamentals will not change much and there is no market-moving news around the corner."
The yuan closed on Friday at 8.2960 against the dollar.

"The key factor on the market is a surplus of dollars, which is not likely to change in the short term," said one foreign exchange analyst. "But this over-supply will be neutralised by central bank intervention."

Analysts said the over-supply was mainly due to China's foreign trade surplus, which hit $3.8 billion for the first two months of 1997 and which the analyst sources said could reach $4.6 billion by the end of March.
China expects a smooth flow of foreign investment this year, and some officials have estimated it will reach $49 billion, up by about 15 percent from 1996's $42.3 billion.
More dollars will be pumped into the Chinese market this month when the local branches of some foreign banks start to do local currency business.

The central bank has given approval to eight overseas banks to do yuan business on certain pre-conditions which include moving their offices to Pudong, Shanghai's premier economic development zone across the Huangpu River from the city centre.
Of the eight, three -- Citibank of the United States, the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd and the Hong Kong & Shanghai Banking Corp -- have already moved to Pudong.
"In our local business, funding is expected to be a key problem," said a banker with one of the approved eight.
"We are very likely to resort to the interbank market as one means of yuan funding," he told Reuters.
"The start of yuan business by foreign banks is likely to add foreign currency supply on the interbank in the short term," said a second interbank market trader.
But analysts said the central bank was not likely to loosen control over the exchange rate on the market.
China's foreign exchange reserves hit a record high of $110 billion in February.
One foreign exchange analyst said the central bank felt reserves of $150 billion would be appropriate for China.
"The central bank has said it will make the currency stable this year and that policy will not change any time soon," he said.
"It (the central bank) is expected to continue to buy dollars on the market," he said.
The foreign exchange market was established in Shanghai in April 1994 and is tightly controlled.
The central bank has an independent trading room on the market, through which it can monitor all transactions and make decisions accordingly.
Other members, in contrast, do not have access to any but their own trades and are thus kept in the dark about general market trends.
